cls: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BCR-ABL and SRC-family kinase inhibitor)
pharm: Oral multikinase inhibitor that blocks BCR-ABL and SRC-family kinases (plus c-KIT, EPHA2, PDGFR-beta), suppressing proliferation of Philadelphia chromosome-positive leukemic cells including many imatinib-resistant clones
quick: Chronic phase CML 100 mg once daily; accelerated/blast phase CML or Ph+ ALL 140 mg once daily
With or without food; avoid grapefruit juice
Can cause fetal harm (hydrops fetalis, fetal cytopenias); avoid and use contraception
Breastfeeding not recommended during and for 2 weeks after last dose
No clinically relevant PK effect; no specific dose adjustment in label
Use with caution; monitor liver function (no specific adjustment given)
No specific interaction listed; avoid if hepatotoxicity concerns
CBCs, LFTs, signs of PAH/fluid retention/bleeding, QTc and electrolytes
summary: Dasatinib is an oral BCR-ABL/SRC-family tyrosine kinase inhibitor used to treat Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) across all phases and Ph+ acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), including disease resistant or intolerant to imatinib. Chronic phase CML in adults is treated with 100 mg once daily and advanced phase CML or Ph+ ALL with 140 mg once daily. It carries important warnings for serious and sometimes fatal bleeding-related events (often tied to thrombocytopenia and platelet dysfunction), myelosuppression, fluid retention including pleural effusion, cardiovascular toxicity, QT prolongation, and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), which can appear even after more than a year of treatment and warrants permanent discontinuation if confirmed.
indications: Newly diagnosed adults with Ph+ chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase
Adults with chronic, accelerated, or myeloid/lymphoid blast phase Ph+ CML with resistance or intolerance to prior therapy including imatinib
Adults with Ph+ acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL) with resistance or intolerance to prior therapy
Pediatric patients 1 year of age and older with Ph+ CML in chronic phase
Pediatric patients 1 year of age and older with newly diagnosed Ph+ ALL, in combination with chemotherapy

dosage.n: May escalate to 140 mg once daily if inadequate hematologic/cytogenetic response; swallow whole, with or without food

dosage.r: Accelerated/blast phase CML or Ph+ ALL
dosage.n: May escalate to 180 mg once daily for inadequate response

dosage.r: Chronic phase CML or newly diagnosed Ph+ ALL
dosage.d: Weight-based: 10 to <20 kg = 40 mg; 20 to <30 kg = 60 mg; 30 to <45 kg = 70 mg; >=45 kg = 100 mg once daily
dosage.t: Ph+ ALL given for up to 2 years with chemotherapy
dosage.n: Recalculate dose every 3 months; tablet dosing not recommended below 10 kg; for Ph+ ALL start on or before day 15 of induction

dosage.d: Reduce: 140 mg dose to 40 mg; 100 mg dose to 20 mg; 70 mg dose to 20 mg daily
dosage.n: Avoid if possible; for 60 mg or 40 mg doses interrupt dasatinib until inhibitor stopped (about 1-week washout)
Avoid strong inducers and St. John's wort; monitor carefully for toxicity if dose raised

admin: Administer orally once daily, in the morning or evening, with or without a meal
Swallow tablets whole - do not crush, cut, or chew
Avoid grapefruit juice and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors/inducers
Do not give H2 antagonists or proton pump inhibitors with dasatinib; if an antacid is needed, give it at least 2 hours before or after the dose
Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before and during therapy
Maintain hydration and correct uric acid before starting in high tumor-burden patients
Handle as a hazardous antineoplastic product; pregnant personnel should avoid crushed/broken tablets
moa: Dasatinib inhibits, at nanomolar concentrations, BCR-ABL and the SRC family of kinases (SRC, LCK, YES, FYN) as well as c-KIT, EPHA2, and PDGFR-beta. By binding multiple conformations of the ABL kinase it suppresses proliferation of CML and ALL cell lines overexpressing BCR-ABL and can overcome many imatinib-resistance mechanisms, including most BCR-ABL kinase-domain mutations and SRC-family pathway activation.

relative: Patients who have or may develop QT prolongation (congenital long QT, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, antiarrhythmics, cumulative high-dose anthracyclines)
Active intercurrent bleeding or concomitant antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy (increased hemorrhage risk)
monitor: Signs of fluid retention / pleural effusion
Bone growth and development in pediatric patients

preg: Based on limited human data, dasatinib can cause fetal harm when given to a pregnant woman. Transplacental transfer occurs, and adverse pharmacologic effects including hydrops fetalis, fetal leukopenia, and fetal thrombocytopenia have been reported with maternal exposure; human experience suggests it may cause congenital malformations including neural tube defects. Animal studies showed embryo-fetal toxicity, fetal death, and skeletal malformations at exposures below human therapeutic levels. Advise pregnant women of the potential risk to the fetus and advise females and males of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during treatment and for 30 days after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on the presence of dasatinib in human milk or its effects on the breastfed child or on milk production; dasatinib is present in the milk of lactating rats. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in a breastfed child, breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment with dasatinib and for 2 weeks after the last dose.
renal: Renal impairment (creatinine clearance about 22 to 342 mL/min) has no clinically relevant effect on dasatinib pharmacokinetics, and the label provides no specific renal dose adjustment.
hepatic: In moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B) mean Cmax fell about 47% and AUC about 8%, and in severe impairment (Child-Pugh C) Cmax fell about 43% and AUC about 28% versus normal liver function. Dasatinib may cause hepatotoxicity; assess liver function before treatment and monthly or as clinically indicated, with closer monitoring when combined with chemotherapy that can affect the liver, and use with caution in hepatic impairment.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole - raised Cmax ~4-fold, AUC ~5-fold) - avoid or reduce dasatinib dose
Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin - lowered Cmax ~81%, AUC ~82%) and St. John's wort - avoid or increase dose
Antiplatelet agents and anticoagulants - increased bleeding risk
QT-prolonging drugs / antiarrhythmics and cumulative high-dose anthracyclines - additive QT risk
moderate: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole - AUC down ~43%) - do not coadminister
H2 antagonists (e.g., famotidine - AUC down ~61%) - do not coadminister
Antacids - separate by at least 2 hours; do not give simultaneously
minor: Dasatinib is a time-dependent CYP3A4 inhibitor and a P-gp substrate
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; a high-fat meal raises AUC by about 14% (not clinically significant)
interactions.alcohol: No specific alcohol interaction described in the label
interactions.diagnostics: Avoid grapefruit juice; correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia before and during therapy to limit QT risk

common: Fluid retention including pleural effusion and peripheral/superficial edema
Headache, fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, myalgia, arthralgia
serious: Serious and fatal bleeding-related events (including GI and CNS hemorrhage), often with severe thrombocytopenia
Severe pleural/pericardial effusion and other severe fluid retention
Cardiovascular toxicity (cardiac ischemia, cardiac dysfunction, arrhythmia, TIA)
rare: Severe mucocutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme)
Growth retardation, delayed epiphyseal fusion, osteopenia, and gynecomastia in children
emergency: Tumor lysis syndrome (nausea, weakness, edema, muscle cramps, seizures)

monitoring: Complete blood counts - chronic phase CML every 2 weeks for 12 weeks then every 3 months; advanced phase CML/Ph+ ALL weekly for 2 months then monthly
Signs and symptoms of bleeding (especially with thrombocytopenia)
Symptoms of fluid retention / pleural effusion (dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, dry cough) - chest x-ray as needed
Cardiopulmonary evaluation for PAH before and during treatment; discontinue permanently if PAH confirmed
Liver function tests at baseline and monthly or as clinically indicated
Uric acid and electrolytes for tumor lysis risk
Bone growth and development in pediatric patients
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed once daily; swallow tablets whole and do not crush, cut, or chew them
Avoid grapefruit juice; if you take antacids, separate them from dasatinib by at least 2 hours, and do not use stomach-acid pills (PPIs/H2 blockers) without your doctor
Report fever or signs of infection promptly because blood counts can drop
Report unusual bleeding or easy bruising right away
Report swelling, weight gain, dry cough, chest pain on breathing, or shortness of breath (possible fluid retention or PAH)
Seek urgent care for chest pain, palpitations, fainting, slurred speech, or transient vision changes
Females and male partners should use effective contraception during treatment and for 30 days after the last dose; do not breastfeed during and for 2 weeks after treatment
pk: Absorbed rapidly; steady state reached quickly with once-daily dosing
Tmax about 0.5 to 6 hours after an oral dose
Mean terminal half-life about 3 to 5 hours
Once-daily dosing; eliminated mainly in feces (about 85%), little renal excretion
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); excursions 15-30 C permitted; child-resistant package; handle as hazardous
pearls: CAUTION - pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH): can occur any time, even after more than 1 year; evaluate cardiopulmonary status before and during therapy and permanently discontinue dasatinib if PAH is confirmed (often reversible on stopping)

CAUTION - bleeding-related events: serious and sometimes fatal hemorrhage (GI most common, also CNS), usually linked to severe thrombocytopenia plus dasatinib-induced platelet dysfunction; antiplatelets/anticoagulants add risk
Fluid retention and pleural effusion are characteristic - more frequent in advanced-phase disease and in older patients; manage with diuretics, dose interruption, or thoracentesis
Chronic phase CML adults = 100 mg once daily; accelerated/blast phase CML and Ph+ ALL = 140 mg once daily
Active against many imatinib-resistant BCR-ABL mutations but NOT the T315I mutation
Correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia to reduce QT-prolongation risk; avoid PPIs/H2 blockers as they markedly lower dasatinib levels
missed: If a dose is missed, do not take an extra dose - simply take the next scheduled dose at its regular time. Do not take two doses at the same time.
overdose: Experience is limited; the highest reported overdose (280 mg/day for 1 week in two patients) caused severe myelosuppression and bleeding. Monitor patients who take more than the recommended dose closely for myelosuppression and give appropriate supportive care; there is no specific antidote.
